lead: Every CMOS chip draws current from its supply for two reasons. When nodes switch, the supply charges their capacitance and that energy ends up as heat: this is dynamic power, and it grows with the clock frequency. Even when nothing switches, transistors that are meant to be off still leak: this is static power. Dynamic power sets how hot a busy processor runs; static power sets how fast an idle phone's battery drains. Both are estimated before layout, because they decide the supply voltage, the clock and the package.
prereq: You need: the CMOS inverter and subthreshold conduction (see Leakage and subthreshold conduction).

blocks.text: When the output of a gate rises, the pMOS draws charge C<sub>L</sub>V<sub>DD</sub> from the supply, which delivers energy C<sub>L</sub>V<sub>DD</sub>². Half, ½C<sub>L</sub>V<sub>DD</sub>², is stored on C<sub>L</sub>; the other half is lost as heat in the pMOS. When the output falls, the nMOS turns the stored half into heat. So each 0 → 1 transition costs C<sub>L</sub>V<sub>DD</sub>² from the supply, whatever the transistor sizes.

Psw = αCLVDD²f Here α is the activity factor: the probability that the node makes a 0 → 1 transition in a clock cycle. f is the clock frequency in Hz. A clock line has α = 1; a signal that toggles every cycle has α = 0.5; random data has α = 0.25.

Short-circuit power. While the input ramps through the band Vtn < Vin < VDD − |Vtp|, both transistors conduct for a moment and current flows straight from VDD to ground. For a symmetric inverter with an input ramp of rise and fall time tr:

Psc ≈ (k/12)(VDD − 2Vt)³trf Here k is the transistor gain in A/V² and Vt the threshold. It is zero if VDD < 2Vt and small when edges are sharp; it is usually kept under about a tenth of Psw by keeping input and output edges similar.
Glitches. When inputs of a gate arrive at different times, its output can switch and switch back in one cycle. Each glitch costs energy like a real transition, so α must count glitches too.
Static power is drawn with all inputs steady. In static CMOS there is no designed path from V<sub>DD</sub> to ground, so only leakage flows:

items: Subthreshold leakage: an off transistor (VGS < Vt) still conducts a little, and the current rises tenfold for every drop of S in Vt. S, the subthreshold swing, is about 60 mV per decade at room temperature in the ideal case and 80 to 100 mV in real devices. It grows quickly with temperature.
Gate leakage: carriers tunnel through a very thin gate oxide; high-k gate dielectrics were introduced to cut it.
Junction leakage: reverse-biased drain and source junctions, including band-to-band tunnelling in heavily doped devices.

blocks.text: Pstatic = VDDIleak Here ileak is the total leakage current of the chip in amperes. Some syllabi call this standby or leakage power.
Ratioed circuits such as NMOS and pseudo-nMOS inverters add a third, much larger static term: the load current that flows whenever their output is low.
P = αCLVDD²f + Psc + VDDIleak Here the first two terms scale with f; the last does not.

At high clock rates the switching term dominates; at low rates, or with the clock stopped, leakage is all that is left. The frequency where the two are equal, f = Ileak/(αCLVDD), tells you which to attack. The supply appears squared in the switching term and also scales leakage, so it is the strongest single knob; the methods that use it are in low-power design.
A power figure is only as good as its α and C. α comes from simulating real workloads; C comes from gate, diffusion and wire capacitance, the same load used for delay.

examples.question: A CMOS block has V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.8 V, total switched capacitance C<sub>L</sub> = 50 pF, f = 100 MHz and α = 0.1. Its leakage current is 10 µA. Find the switching power, the leakage power, the total, and the frequency at which the two are equal. Neglect short-circuit power.
steps: Crossover: f = I<sub>leak</sub>/(αC<sub>L</sub>V<sub>DD</sub>) = 10 × 10⁻⁶/(0.1 × 50 × 10⁻¹² × 1.8) = 1.11 MHz. Below about 1.1 MHz leakage is the larger part (Figure 3.7.1).
examples.answer: P<sub>sw</sub> = 1.62 mW, P<sub>leak</sub> = 18 µW, total 1.638 mW; the two are equal at about 1.11 MHz.

examples.question: To gain speed, the same block is moved to transistors whose threshold is 100 mV lower. The subthreshold swing is S = 100 mV per decade and subthreshold current dominates the leakage. Find the new leakage power and the new crossover frequency.
steps: A 100 mV drop in V<sub>t</sub> with S = 100 mV/decade raises the subthreshold current by 10<sup>100/100</sup> = 10 times: 10 µA → 100 µA.
At 100 MHz the total becomes 1.62 + 0.18 = 1.80 mW, 10% more for the same work.
examples.answer: Leakage rises tenfold to 180 µW and the crossover moves up to 11.1 MHz.

traps: Leaving out α: C<sub>L</sub>V<sub>DD</sub>²f is the power of a clock line, not of an average node.
Defining α as all transitions and still using C V²f; with that definition the formula needs a factor of ½. State which α you use.
Putting f into the leakage term. Static power is VDD × I<sub>leak</sub>.
Calling short-circuit power static. It flows only while inputs are moving.
Saying half the energy is lost only if the transistor is small. The ½CV² loss per charge is independent of the resistance.

quiz.a: The probability that a node makes a 0 → 1 transition in a clock cycle; it is dimensionless and 1 for a clock.

quiz.q: Why does one 0 → 1 transition draw C<sub>L</sub>V<sub>DD</sub>² from the supply although only ½C<sub>L</sub>V<sub>DD</sub>² is stored?
quiz.a: The supply delivers charge C<sub>L</sub>V<sub>DD</sub> at voltage V<sub>DD</sub>, which is C<sub>L</sub>V<sub>DD</sub>² of energy. Half is stored on the capacitor and half is turned into heat in the pMOS while charging.

quiz.q: V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.2 V, C = 30 pF, f = 200 MHz and α = 0.05. Find P<sub>sw</sub>.
An inverter has k = 100 µA/V², V<sub>t</sub> = 0.5 V, V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.8 V, t<sub>r</sub> = 100 ps and f = 100 MHz. Estimate its short-circuit power.
Name the three leakage mechanisms and one cause of each.
quiz.a: Subthreshold: an off transistor still conducts below V<sub>t</sub>. Gate: tunnelling through thin oxide. Junction: reverse-biased drain and source junctions.

quiz.q: At 1 MHz a chip has 10 mW dynamic and 5 mW leakage power. What are they at 100 MHz, and which dominates at each frequency?
quiz.a: Dynamic power scales with f: 1 W at 100 MHz, while leakage stays 5 mW. Dynamic dominates at both, by 2 to 1 at 1 MHz and 200 to 1 at 100 MHz.

quiz.q: Why do sharp input edges reduce short-circuit power but not switching power?
quiz.a: Short-circuit current flows only while the input is between the two thresholds, so a shorter ramp shortens it. Switching energy is C<sub>L</sub>V<sub>DD</sub>² per transition, whatever the edge rate.

beyond: Not for the exam. Power sign-off tools read switching activity from simulation files (SAIF or VCD) and compute power per net and per block, then check that the hottest spot stays within the package limit. Since about 2005, when supply voltages stopped falling with each process generation, power rather than transistor count has limited chip clock speeds. Search next for SAIF power analysis, the end of Dennard scaling and dark silicon.

figure.caption: Power of the example block against clock frequency on log scales. Switching power rises in proportion to f and passes 1.62 mW at 100 MHz; leakage is flat, so below the crossover (1.11 MHz, or 11.1 MHz with the lower-threshold transistors) leakage is the larger part.
